column1: Why must hardware peripheral registers be declared `volatile` in C firmware?
column2: To prevent the compiler from optimizing away or reordering reads/writes, since the memory location has hardware side effects beyond simple storage (e.g., triggering a transfer or reflecting changing hardware state).

column1: What architectural model do ARM Cortex-M processors use for peripheral access, and how does it differ from x86 isolated I/O?
column2: Memory-mapped I/O: peripherals occupy fixed addresses in the same 4GB address space as RAM (e.g., SRAM at 0x20000000, peripherals at 0x40000000). x86 isolated I/O uses separate address spaces with dedicated IN/OUT instructions.

column1: What is the core invariant that necessitates critical sections in interrupt-driven firmware?
column2: Atomicity under asynchronicity: an ISR can interrupt code at any instruction boundary, so shared data accessed by both main code and ISRs can be corrupted without disabling interrupts (masking) during access.

column1: What is priority inversion in the context of interrupt/RTOS scheduling?
column2: A scenario where a high-priority task is blocked waiting on a resource held by a low-priority task, effectively letting lower-priority work delay higher-priority execution.

column1: How does an RTOS scheduler's philosophy toward low-priority tasks fundamentally differ from a general-purpose OS scheduler?
column2: An RTOS will deliberately starve low-priority tasks indefinitely if higher-priority work keeps arriving, prioritizing temporal correctness over fairness; general-purpose OSes implement fairness policies to prevent starvation.

column1: What is Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) and why does it exclude dynamic memory allocation and garbage collection from RTOS critical paths?
column2: WCET is the statically analyzable upper bound on an operation's execution time. malloc() traverses free lists of unpredictable length and GC introduces stop-the-world pauses—both inject unbounded latency that violates deterministic timing guarantees.

column1: What are the three interlocking mechanisms a device driver uses to mediate CPU-peripheral communication?
column2: 1) Managing control/status registers via MMIO reads/writes, 2) coordinating data movement (polled, interrupt-driven, or DMA-based), 3) enforcing synchronization invariants (e.g., memory visibility before DMA transfers, preventing ISR races).

column1: Why is DMA necessary for high-throughput peripheral transfers instead of polled I/O?
column2: Polled I/O wastes CPU cycles waiting on peripheral status and creates latency jitter; DMA offloads data movement to a dedicated controller, freeing the CPU and enabling background transfers for high-throughput or latency-critical workloads.

column1: Why does flash memory require block erasure before reprogramming, unlike SRAM/DRAM?
column2: Flash cells can only transition from a programmed (0) state back to erased (1) state through a block-level erase operation; arbitrary byte-level read-modify-write is not physically supported, unlike RAM's byte-addressable access.

column1: What critical challenge must a bootloader's flash update mechanism solve given flash memory's physical constraints and lack of hardware transaction support?
column2: It must maintain atomic update semantics (e.g., via dual-bank or A/B partitioning) despite the risk that power failures can interrupt multi-second erase operations, since there is no hardware-level rollback for partial writes.

column1: State the active power consumption model for embedded silicon and identify its two orthogonal control levers.
column2: P_active = C_eff · V² · f + I_leak · V. The two levers are: (1) dynamic power management via frequency/voltage scaling, and (2) static power management via clock gating or power domain shutdown.

column1: How does a watchdog timer detect and recover from firmware hangs, and what must firmware do to prevent an unwanted reset?
column2: A watchdog is a counter that decrements each clock tick and triggers a system reset upon underflow to zero. Firmware must periodically 'kick' (reload) the counter to prove forward progress/liveness; failure to do so (e.g., due to an infinite loop or deadlock) triggers deterministic recovery via reset.
